::: {.why}
The six numbers you wrote down last night contain the whole reason stochastic calculus exists, and everything in the next five weeks is a consequence of one of those two columns being non-zero.
:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State what the quadratic variation of Brownian motion over an interval equals, and demonstrate it numerically.
- Say why a smooth function has zero quadratic variation and what that implies for the chain rule.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Interpret your numbers: the sum of squared increments converges to the length of the interval, and the sum of absolute increments diverges. Repeat both for a smooth function such as a sine wave over the same interval and confirm the squared sum goes to zero there. That contrast is the definition of the problem.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [25 min]{.task-min} Read the section of the CMU stochastic calculus notes on quadratic variation, then write the informal identity that the square of a Brownian increment behaves like the time increment. This is the one line you will use in every derivation for the next month, so write it somewhere permanent.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Check the corollary: the cross-variation of Brownian motion with time, and the quadratic variation of time itself, are both zero. Verify both numerically so that the three rules are facts you have seen rather than a table you memorised.
:::
:::
